    Latest Update: Hyatt Adds Stackable Awards, But Globalists Lose Free Parking Benefit

    📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1058 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Liveandletsfly

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Recent findings suggest that world of Hyatt is adding newly introduced Milestone Rewards and allowing members to combine awards starting in 2027.
    • Industry observers note that hyatt has announced changes beginning January 1, 2027, that will give members more ways to earn and redeem rewards.
    • Sources indicate that globalists currently receive complimentary parking on eligible award nights at participating hotels where parking can be charged to the room.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that world of Hyatt is adding newly introduced Milestone Rewards and allowing members to combine awards starting in 2027. There is plenty to like, particularly the ability to apply a suite upgrade to a free night certificate. But Globalists will lose automatic free parking on award stays, and a uniform one-year expiration will make some awards harder to use.

    Industry observers note that hyatt has announced changes beginning January 1, 2027, that will give members more ways to earn and redeem rewards. But there are concessions here too, especially for frequent guests who already make good use of the existing benefits.

    Let’s start with the parking change.

    Sources indicate that globalists currently receive complimentary parking on eligible award nights at participating hotels where parking can be charged to the room. That can be a substantial benefit, particularly at city hotels and resorts with expensive parking.

    Sources indicate that hyatt is replacing that status benefit with a selectable Free Parking Award, first available at 60 qualifying nights or 100,000 Base Points. Each award will cover one qualifying stay of up to seven nights and can be gifted. The improvement is that the award will work on eligible paid stays too. The drawback is that members must select it instead of another reward.

    Hyatt tells Live And Let’s Fly:.

    “This decision was made as 70% of Globalists did not use the free parking benefit in 2025; 95% used it 4 times or less, and moving this to a choice allowed the program to retain it for members who value it and introduce other exciting new awards like the $200 Thompson Hotels Credit and the $500 Premium Suite Credit.”.

    After that, Globalist status alone will not provide free parking.

    I appreciate the advance notice, but this is a devaluation for members who regularly drive to Hyatt properties and redeem points, a benefit I used regularly when I was still Globalist and still use on Guest of Honor awards today.

    It has been revealed that the ability to stack eligible awards is the most appealing part of this announcement and is a very positive change. Starting in 2027, members can combine a Suite Upgrade Award with a free night certificate, including Category 1–4, Category 1–7, Ultimate Free Night, and other eligible promotional certificates.

    Industry observers note that that addresses a frustrating restriction and having both a free night and a suite upgrade in your account should make it easier to plan a special stay. Other eligible combinations will include Suite Upgrade Awards, Guest of Honor Awards, and Free Parking Awards on the same reservation.

    It has been revealed that for someone without Globalist status, combining a confirmed suite with Guest of Honor benefits could make for a very nice stay. For a Globalist, being able to confirm a suite while using a free night certificate is also very useful.

    Sources indicate that there are still restrictions. For example, the new Thompson Hotels and Premium Suite credits cannot be combined with a Free Night Award (I address the new milestone awards below). Hyatt has published the details on its 2027 updates page.

    Awards issued beginning January 1, 2027, will expire 365 days after issuance.

    That makes the rules easier to remember, but whether it helps depends on the award.

    Recent findings suggest that some milestone free night certificates presently expire after 180 days. Doubling that window is welcome…six months can pass very rapidly when you are trying to find the right opportunity to use a certificate.

    Sources indicate that but Suite Upgrade Awards, Club Access Awards, and Guest of Honor Awards right now can remain valid considerably longer, through the end of February of the second calendar year after they are earned. Reducing those to one year is a loss. Even today as I look to book stays in January and February of next year, I’ll be using those “older” Guest of Honor Awards.

    That said, I would not call this change unreasonable and for most people it will be a net positive.

    Milestone Rewards will begin at 10 qualifying nights or 20,000 Base Points, with additional milestones every 10 nights through 150.

    Here are some notable new choices (which are in addition to the existing choices):.

    Sources indicate that the $500 Premium Suite Credit awarded at 100 nights requires an eligible paid stay of at least two nights. I would evaluate that against what I would otherwise spend…a discount on an expensive suite is only useful if you would not otherwise get the upgrade anyway as a Globalist.

    There are other trade-offs worth noting.

    At 50 nights, the suite upgrade choice drops from two awards to one.

    It has been revealed that at 60 nights, My Hyatt Concierge becomes a selection rather than an automatic benefit (a worthless benefit, in my opinion). Members will choose two rewards from a menu that also includes suite upgrades, parking, points, and a skimpy Delta eCertificate.

    If you value your concierge and want to retain the suite upgrades, that leaves no selection for parking….

    The fresh Delta partnership adds eCertificates at milestones from 20–60 nights, two single-visit Sky Club passes at 70, 80, and 90 nights, and Medallion status options at higher thresholds. Of course the Delta Air Lines awards replace the American Airlines awards.

    Members will need to link their Hyatt and Delta accounts. Hyatt is also enhancing “Pay My Way” so members can choose awards, points, cash, or Points + Cash for individual nights within a stay.

    Hyatt’s technology has long lagged, but this is a nice newly introduced revision.

    The ability to combine free night certificates with suite upgrades is an excellent change. Earlier milestones and additional reward choices should also give members more opportunities to find something useful.

    It has been revealed that but the parking change is a loss for Globalists who regularly use that benefit. Shorter validity for some awards, fewer suite upgrades at 50 nights, and making concierge access a choice deserve attention too, as much I always loathed my own concierge agents.

    I appreciate that Hyatt is providing notice and protecting existing parking benefits during the transition. All in all, I’d say these changes are positive, but will hurt some travelers a lot more than others.

    My favorite thing about San Juan? You can have a morning that feels plucked out of a history book, an afternoon that commits you entirely to the beach, and a night that’s topped off with a frosty Medalla, sweet rum cocktail, and flirty bachata dance. It’s glitzy yet lush, historic yet ever-evolving, a city delightfully full of contrasts, and one I will never run out of reasons to revisit.

    According to recent reports, my father’s side of the family is from Puerto Rico, so I’ve been coming back to the island for years, and I love that there’s always another corner to get to know. There’s Old San Juan, with all its pastel-painted façades, galleries and shops, blue cobblestone streets, and tucked-away restaurants; Condado and Ocean Park for long, sea-salty afternoons by the ocean; and Santurce, where street murals, galleries, haute dining, and a lively bar scene bring a fresh, creative vibe to the city.

    Sources indicate that of course, there’s no shortage of hotels in San Juan, but sometimes a vacation to the island’s capital calls for a little more room to sprawl, or a front door that opens onto a lush little neighborhood rather than a buzzy hotel lobby. The city’s best Airbnbs offer just that, along with wonderful amenities, whether it’s a private pool hidden behind swaying palms or a breezy courtyard for sipping on some local morning coffee.

    According to recent reports, consider this your invitation to soak up the sun in Puerto Rico's capital for a few days. Read on for nine of the best Airbnbs in San Juan to consider for your next trip.

    We've selected these listings based on Superhost status, ratings, amenities, location, decor, editor stays, and previous guest reviews.

    Number of guests: 5Bed and bath: 2 bedrooms, 1 bathWhy we love it: Unique design, proximity to the beach, city skyline views, fully equipped kitchen.

You’ll never be bored at this retro-inspired haven, what with its groovy wallpaper in nearly every room, playful lava lamps, disco ball, and hanging plants. Conveniently, it's situated right in the heart of San Juan’s food and arts district and just a few steps from Ocean Park Beach. If you do decide to stay in for the night, rinse off the sand in your designer rain shower, throw a vinyl on the record player, and cook up some local produce in the fully stocked kitchen. Thanks to the in-unit washer and dryer, you’ll likely depart with no dirty beach laundry. As for the sleeping arrangements? The space can fit up to five guests, but there’s only two bedrooms. So if you’re doubling up, the fifth guest would have to crash on the living room’s sofa bed.

    Neighborhood: SanturceThings to do nearby: Ocean Park, Calle Loiza, Museo de Arte de Puerto Rico.

This central Carolina base is for those seeking out an easy, breezy group trip, whether traveling with friends or family. The bedrooms have just what you need to feel at home; two offer a queen bed, and the third fits in two singles. Perhaps the biggest perk of all: The back of the house is lined with floor-to-ceiling glass doors, which open out to the small-but-mighty backyard, where a plunge pool that doubles as an outdoor bar will tempt you to stay a while.

    According to recent reports, design-minded travelers, consider this lush oasis with interiors inspired by the Mediterranean. After a day of venturing to the capital city, its thoughtful touches make relaxing in style that much easier: Cool off in the outdoor shower, escape the island heat in the AC, or sway in the hammock with a good book. When it’s time to unwind, cue up a film on the living room's projector, or head to either of the two bedrooms, where queen beds and smart TVs await.

Each of the bedrooms is roomy, and you’ll find a separate dining area for meals at home, a bright and airy living room to talk about all your adventures from the day, and a sleek kitchen with deep green cabinets. Outside, hang out on the backyard patio to read or listen to music in the hammock surrounded by swaying palms, and take in this midcentury-modern home—there aren’t many like this in the capital with this much space and access to the finer things of the city. (Yes, remarked finer things do include heading to La Placita to get your bachata on.).

The hosts note they drew design inspiration from the “serene and vibrant colors of the city’s golden hour and sunsets”—views you and your crew can soak in from a rooftop bar in Old San Juan, a 15-minute drive away, on Isla Verde Beach 10 minutes away, or poolside in your very own backyard.

But try to commit to the bit and fall into the old-school sentiment with a more analog stay. Meaning? Quit the scrolling. Instead, play some tunes on the record player, dance under the disco ball, unwind on the front porch’s swing chair, and jump right into the comfy, ergonomic mattress. When it’s time to head out, you’re in walking distance of the beach and a quick drive to the sweet cobblestone streets of Old San Juan.

    Neighborhood: SanturceThings to do nearby: Ocean Park Beach, Calle Loíza, Las Marias, Playa del Pueblo, Old San Juan.

    Number of guests: 3Bed and bath: 1 bedroom, 1 bathWhy we love it: Rain shower, private patio, indoor hammock, design-forward, walkable to beach.

    Industry observers note that in the mood for some island romance? There’s no better place for love than this gorgeous apartment with the sea in easy reach. With interiors curated by Dreamers Welcome, a Puerto Rico–based hospitality group focused on luxury stays with a laid-back vibe, you’ll also have exclusive access to amenities at nearby boutique hotel Dreamcatcher by DW. This includes a daily vegan or vegetarian breakfast, guided tours, yoga on the beach, and a gift store to shop at with crafts by local creatives. Back at the apartment, take in the views from the intimate patio space, sway on the indoor hammock, and fall into the ever-cozy sofa. With a double vanity and rich red polished shower, even a trip to the bathroom here will make you feel like you’re in a design magazine.

    Neighborhood: SanturceThings to do nearby: Condado, Ocean Park, Old San Juan, Museo de Arte de Puerto Rico, Miramar.

    Number of guests: 8Bed and bath: 4 bedrooms, 3 bathsWhy we love it: Private pool, barbecue, outdoor seating area, beach access, kid-friendly amenities.

Just steps from the Ocean Park beach—where you’re sure to see kitesurfers aplenty—you’ll also have a pool to lounge in and around right at home.     Review: Austrian Airlines A320 Economy Class

    📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1068 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Liveandletsfly

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • After a lovely stay in Vienna, we continued our journey to Zürich onboard an Austrian Airlines A320 in economy class.
    • We arrived at the airport around 9:30 am, figuring there would be no need to get there early to use a lounge when we had just enjoyed an excellent breakfast at the Park Hyatt Vienna.
    • The airport was busy but we used the Star Gold corridor to enjoy expedited security and were soon at the gate, ready to board our short flight to Switzerland.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    After a lovely stay in Vienna, we continued our journey to Zürich onboard an Austrian Airlines A320 in economy class.

    We arrived at the airport around 9:30 am, figuring there would be no need to get there early to use a lounge when we had just enjoyed an excellent breakfast at the Park Hyatt Vienna.

    The airport was busy but we used the Star Gold corridor to enjoy expedited security and were soon at the gate, ready to board our short flight to Switzerland.

    Stepping onboard, we headed to the back to find our seats in row 22.

    The Austrian A320 has 180 seats arranged in a 3-3 configuration (same in business class, though the middle seat is blocked).

    The Recaro BL3520 “NEK” slimline seats are very uncomfortable with very little padding. These are familiar seats if you have flown within Europe on Lufthansa Group carriers, with a literature pocket and a folding tray table on the seatback ahead.

    Legroom varies by aircraft and row. Austrian lists a minimum economy class seat pitch of just 28 inches across its A320 fleet, so do not expect much room to stretch out, though it felt like we had 29 inches.

    In a recent development, there are no power ports or USB ports on this aircraft. Thankfully, however, there are individual air vents, unlike on the 777.

    In economy class, passengers receive a free glass of water and Austrian chocolate.

    For those peckish, buy-on-board is available. I pre-ordered a hot meal from the carrier’s Austrian Melangerie menu.

    Industry observers note that what else would I order on Austrian Airlines but Wiener Schnitzel? While a proper Wiener Schnitzel is made with veal, Austrian uses chicken onboard, describing the dish as:.

    Golden-brown chicken schnitzel with parsley potatoes.

    The price was €13.80, though I received a 10% discount for pre-ordering.

    Presentation was very much like economy class: the schnitzel and potatoes were served together in a cardboard box, but sometimes you have to look beyond the presentation. The chicken was tender, the breading remained surprisingly crisp, and the parsley potatoes were a nice accompaniment…my son Augustine and I both enjoyed it.

    I highlighted this meal in a recent Meal of the Week feature.

    > Read More: Austrian Airlines’ €13.80 Wiener Schnitzel On An 80-Minute Flight.

    Recent findings suggest that I had also hoped to try the Julius Meinl Wiener Melange, a €5.20 coffee served with milk foam in a proper ceramic cup on a silver tray. Alas, Austrian only offers the Melange on flights of at least 80 minutes and our Vienna to Zürich flight was apparently five minutes too short according to the flight attendant.

    Before landing I used the lavatory in the rear of the aircraft and it was messy by that point, with paper towels overflowing from the waste receptacle.

    Sources indicate that while there is no seatback screens or streaming movies and TV indicates, Wi-Fi was available for purchase onboard. A high speed pass (Viasat) was 6€ while messaging was free. I had trouble connecting, initially, but ultimately was able to pay the 6€ and connect.

    This was a quick, boring flight with a delicious lunch onboard thanks to the buy-on-board menu. I’d never go out of my way to fly Austrian shorthaul in economy class, but if you are stuck behind the curtain, do take advantage of the pre-order menu to make the flight go by a bit faster.

    My original review, covering an Austrian Airlines A320 journey from Vienna to Yerevan, Armenian (fun trip!) in 2019 is below.

    What is Austrian Airlines like on a mid-haul flight in economy class?

    In a recent development, my business partner, John, and I spent a weekend in Yerevan, Armenia last month. We were in Vienna earlier in the week, so the nonstop Austrian flight from VIE to EVN made the most sense. We booked for 15,000 United miles each in economy class.

    Business class would have been an extra 10,000 miles, but I figured 1.) the seat is the same, 2.) I already had lounge access, and 3.) we would be eating dinner just before the flight. So the upgrade did not make sense.

    Vienna International Airport is such an easy airport to navigate. Check-in (John had to check a bag), security, and passport control took only a few moments. I’ll review the Austrian lounge in a separate post.

    Boarding commenced precisely on schedule with business class passenger and Star Alliance Gold members invited to board first.

    I’ll start with the seats and the following warning: these slimline seats are very uncomfortable. By the time we reached Yerevan three hours later, I could not wait to get off. The seats do recline slightly, but the lack of padding makes for an uncomfortable flying experience on flights longer than 60-90 minutes. But that’s hardly a unique experience to Austrian. Seat pitch is 30 inches.

    Notice that the only difference in business class hard product is that the middle seat is blocked:.

    Recent findings suggest that A sticker on the aircraft fuselage indicated wi-fi internet would be available, but it did not function. There are no in-seat power ports.

    But Austrian does a few things right.

    First, I appreciated the pillows and blankets, both of which were better than many airlines offer in economy class. Heck, United does not even offer pillows in domestic first class except on premium transcontinental flight.

    That said, it was roasting outside and the cabin was not overly cool…not exactly heavy blanket weather.

    Recent findings suggest that second, I appreciated the meal, as small as it was. A vegetarian cheese pasta with cake and bread was served after takeoff. Talk about a load of carbs! Passengers were not offered a choice of meal.

    Flight attendants came around before the meal and also about 90 minutes before landing with a beverage serevice.

    Finally, the lavatory was very clean…these pictures are toward the end of the flight.

    Recent findings suggest that I appreciate that Austrian is full service in the sense that blankets, pillows, and meals are provided. But three hours really pushes the limit for this type of slimline seat. I’ll happily fly Austrian again, but ideally on a shorthaul route or on a widebody jet in business class….

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Alaska Airlines will drop four destinations from its network in Portland, Oregon.

    Sources indicate that the carrier confirmed it will end service from Portland to Baltimore, St. Louis, Fresh Orleans, and Jackson Hole, Wyoming.

    Three of the connections launched only months ago. Portland-Jackson Hole came online in June, and service to Baltimore and St. Louis started in May.

    “As we add fresh routes to our network, we constantly assess existing routes to ensure we’re using our aircraft in the markets our guests want most,” the carrier said in a statement provided to AirlineGeeks. “As part of that process, we’ve made the decision to discontinue service between Portland and Baltimore, Jackson Hole, St. Louis, and New Orleans. We remain committed to Portland and will continue to invest in opportunities that strengthen our network there, including adding service in markets where we see the greatest opportunities for our guests.”.

    Alaska serves over 60 destinations from Portland, and recently opened a new lounge there.

    Finding Unexpected Joy In Music And Hospitality From Los Angeles To Malibu

    📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (524 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Liveandletsfly

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • One of the beautiful things about traveling around the world is the chance to experience hospitality in different ways in different countries.
    • I listen to music during the day as I work on this blog and on my other work.
    • As I listened to her music all morning, one of her YouTube shorts noted that she would be performing a classical concert in Los Angeles, which immediately piqued my interest.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    One of the beautiful things about traveling around the world is the chance to experience hospitality in different ways in different countries. I’ll never forget the hospitality I experienced In Iran or in Ukraine, but sometimes we don’t have to travel far to experience it, as I recently found out in Los Angeles.

    I listen to music during the day as I work on this blog and on my other work. Some people require absolute silence to work, but I like music, specially Christian hymns. I primarily use YouTube and of course the algorithm gets to know you. There’s no music I like more than a powerful organ playing a beloved hymn. Lately, the algorithm has been suggesting a very gifted organist named Lauma Akmene, a Latvian-born musician who is the organist, conductor, and music director at St. Peter’s Episcopal Church in Salisbury, Maryland.

    As I listened to her music all morning, one of her YouTube shorts noted that she would be performing a classical concert in Los Angeles, which immediately piqued my interest.

    I obtained a ticket and found the concert would be held at a place called Stan’s Musical Parlor, which was actually a beautiful 1926 home in LA’s posh Lafayette Square neighborhood. Not knowing quite what to expect, I revealed up and was warmly greeted by Stanley Harris himself, who I came to find out has opened his house since 1986 to showcase musical talents. Dr. Harris is a retired psychiatrist and was a longtime clinician and faculty member at the University of Southern California.

    Stan has a Johannus-BachMen-Hauptwerk organ (including Hauptwerk virtual pipe organs) in his living room. Essentially, this digital organ can be set to emulate sounds from many of famous pipe organs around the world.

    The concert began at 8:00 pm and was simply fabulous, with Lauma playing several classic and neo-classic works.

    One of the guests mentioned that he was hosting Lauma the following evening at his home in Malibu, and invited me to attend. I had to be in Palm Springs for work that day, but I drove from Palms Springs all the way to Malibu via Pacific Coast Highway (took about three hours!) and made it just in time for the concert, another fabulous evening of food, fellowship, and great music.

    It has been revealed that already, I’ve made friends through these two events, who I am staying in touch with, and will go to more of these concerts. Community is beautiful thing, as is hospitality, and all in my backyard, one of the many reasons I love Los Angeles and Southern California so much.

    Truth be told, I almost did not go to either event. I was tired and probably could have used a couple extra hours of sleep. But I’m so glad I did go and I’m thankful to YouTube for suggesting Lauma and making these two possible in the first place.

    Lauma is such a gifted organist. If you like classical music and especially sacred music, you can enjoy her work here.

    https://youtube.com/shorts/tzW8IZxwwN0?si=yodFyoHDSRhOjD9F.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Artificial intelligence could be playing a role in the cascade of high-profile technology failures seen over the last week, U.S. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said Monday.

    Mullin told FOX News’ Sean Hannity that he spoke with someone in the tech industry, “one guy who is very smart with tech,” who identified AI as a possible culprit.

    “He mentioned, ‘I believe that it’s the SI, because the programs aren’t designed to work as fast as SI is,'” he said.

    The individual suggested that the technology’s ability to move fast and fix itself created “ripple effects” that overwhelmed older conventional systems. The secretary noted that theory “kind of makes sense to me.”.

    The Trump administration uses the term “super intelligence,” or SI, in place of AI.

    Mullin said his source did not want to be identified but ruled out at least one famous personality from the tech sector.

    Multiple large, U.S.-based networks have crashed over the past week, including the FAA’s air traffic control communications system, United’s internal applications, Microsoft’s business services, and software used by banks such as JPMorgan Chase and Wells Fargo.

    Mullin noted there is no indication from the intelligence and cybersecurity communities that the outages are part of a cyberattack.

    The FAA has blamed Friday’s nationwide ground stop on a faulty or improperly installed router, which flooded other routers with data and ultimately crashed the system.

    Tech Report: Former Washington Rep. Jim McDermott dies at 89

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • In a recent development, former Rep.
    • Jim McDermott, D-Wash., a fierce advocate for universal health care and outspoken war critic who served 28 years in Congress, died Thursday at the age of 89, his family announced.
    • In a roughly 50-year career in state and federal office, the salty-tongued, liberal lawmaker from Seattle won both praise and criticism for pushing an aggressive agenda focused on expanding health care to all Americans.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In a recent development, former Rep. Jim McDermott, D-Wash., is seen in a vineyard near his cottage in Civrac-en-Médoc, France, on March 20, 2024. (Ariel Cohen/CQ Roll Call).

    Sources indicate that former Rep. Jim McDermott, D-Wash., a fierce advocate for universal health care and outspoken war critic who served 28 years in Congress, died Thursday at the age of 89, his family announced.

    In a roughly 50-year career in state and federal office, the salty-tongued, liberal lawmaker from Seattle won both praise and criticism for pushing an aggressive agenda focused on expanding health care to all Americans.

    As the top Democrat on the House Ways and Means Health Subcommittee, McDermott defended the 2010 Affordable Care Act that expanded health insurance to millions of Americans, while critics complained it did little to control costs.

    “Jim was one of the first and most powerful voices fighting to fix our broken health care system in Congress,” Sen. Patty Murray, D-Wash., wrote on X. “He was passionate and fearless — and left a tremendous legacy on WA state and its people. My thoughts are with Congressman McDermott’s family and loved ones during this difficult time.”.

    When McDermott revealed his retirement from Congress in 2016, then-President Barack Obama praised him in a statement as “a much-needed voice for his most vulnerable constituents.”.

    Born and raised in Illinois, McDermott came from a poor, conservative and deeply religious family. His father, a bond underwriter, and his mother, a telephone operator and homemaker, started a church in the garage of their two-bedroom home. His three siblings slept in one bedroom; his parents in the other. McDermott, the oldest child, had the couch.

    Recent findings suggest that he attended the conservative evangelical Wheaton College. His bend toward liberalism began during medical school at the University of Illinois, when he voted for John F. Kennedy in the 1960 presidential election. After a stint in the U.S. Navy Medical Corps from 1968-1970, McDermott won his first seat in the Washington state House in 1970 running on an anti-war platform.

    He continued his anti-war stances in Congress, voting against the 2002 resolution authorizing the use of military force in Iraq. In 2013, he opposed U.S. intervention in Syria and was one of only 20 House members to vote against new sanctions on Iran.

    Shortly after he retired from Congress, McDermott settled on a newly introduced life for himself by moving to a small town in southwestern France, where he admired some of the public policies he had fought hard to deliver in Washington with mixed success.

    “I spent 16 years in the Washington state legislature trying to get single-payer health care,” he recalled in a 2024 interview with CQ Roll Call at his home about 90 minutes outside of Bourdeaux. “Then I spent nearly 30 years in Congress trying to get single-payer. Then I came to France and in three months I had single-payer. Was that mind-blowing? You bet.”.

    As he noted, McDermott dedicated much time in the Washington state legislature to trying to create a single-payer system. When that didn’t work out, he developed the Washington State Basic Health Program, a health coverage system for the unemployed and working poor — the first state program of its kind.

    In a recent development, then, once he got to Washington, he tried to work with then-First Lady Hillary Clinton to hatch a federal single-payer program, but that effort came to naught. He later backed the Affordable Care Act and tried to pass his own legislation in 2015 for comprehensive health care coverage.

    “The only way to truly ensure that access to quality health care is a right enjoyed by every American is through a single-payer system,” he said in a statement at the time.

    McDermott will also be remembered for some of the attacks he leveled against Republicans. In the most notorious incident, he was ordered to pay then-Rep. John A. Boehner of Ohio — who later became speaker — nearly $1.1 million in 2008 after releasing a recording of a 1996 cell phone call between Boehner and then-Speaker Newt Gingrich. McDermott maintained it was worth the fight, and the cost of the settlement, to protect free speech.

    “Jim McDermott was as big as it gets in Washington state politics,” Sen. Maria Cantwell, D-Wash., wrote on Facebook. “Smart, funny, and Irish, Jim McDermott will be missed.”.

    #6973. Airline Flew Passengers To The Wrong City, Blamed The Weather, Then Admitted The Truth Three Years Later

    📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (765 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Liveandletsfly ↗ Open Full Page

    Airline Flew Passengers To The Wrong City, Blamed The Weather, Then Admitted The Truth Three Years Later

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (765 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Liveandletsfly

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • According to recent reports, an airline flew passengers to the wrong city, welcomed them to the city they were supposed to reach, then blamed bad weather for the detour.
    • Speaking at the World Public Relations Forum in Abuja on November 17, 2026, United Nigeria Airlines Executive Chairman Obiora Okonkwo acknowledged that his organization made an operational failure worse by issuing an inaccurate explanation.
    • According to PUNCH, Okonkwo said a dispatcher entered the wrong destination in the flight documentation.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    According to recent reports, an airline flew passengers to the wrong city, welcomed them to the city they were supposed to reach, then blamed bad weather for the detour. Now the chairman of United Nigeria Airlines is revisiting that embarrassing episode as a lesson in why companies should tell the truth. I agree with that lesson, though I have a few questions about the flight itself….

    Speaking at the World Public Relations Forum in Abuja on November 17, 2026, United Nigeria Airlines Executive Chairman Obiora Okonkwo acknowledged that his organization made an operational failure worse by issuing an inaccurate explanation.

    According to PUNCH, Okonkwo said a dispatcher entered the wrong destination in the flight documentation. The pilots flew to that destination, while the cabin crew apparently believed they had reached the city printed on the passenger tickets.

    The airline then blamed the weather. The flight occurred in November 2023. This week’s news is the chairman discussing the false explanation and the damage it caused.

    On November 26, 2023, United Nigeria Airlines flight 0504 was supposed to carry passengers from Lagos (LOS) to Abuja (ABV), the Nigerian capital. Instead, it landed in Asaba (ABB), 197 nautical miles away.

    Recent findings suggest that that would have been confusing enough, but passengers reported that the cabin crew welcomed them to Abuja after landing. Imagine looking out the window and realizing that the airport does not quite match the announcement….

    According to reporting at the time, passengers noted the pilot subsequently explained that he had received the wrong flight initiative. The aircraft eventually continued to Abuja. But the airline’s public explanation was different. It attributed the stop in Asaba to “poor destination weather” and said an incorrect cabin announcement had caused the confusion.

    Nigeria’s aviation minister, Festus Keyamo, challenged the explanation in November 2023. He said there was no bad weather in Abuja and described the incident as an administrative problem. Keyamo also said a review of air traffic control communications showed that the pilot intended to fly to Asaba.

    Industry observers note that I suppose that is some consolation: the issue was not that the pilots somehow mistook one airport for another while trying to land in Abuja. According to the accounts from the minister and now the airline chairman, the cockpit was operating toward the correct destination acceding to the flight plan, just the wrong destination the carrier was supposed to fly to.

    Recent findings suggest that but that does not make the situation reassuring. It raises a different question: how did the discrepancy survive the preparations for departure?

    Okonkwo’s remarks this week focused on communication. As The Guardian (Nigeria) reports, he acknowledged that the airline’s communications team blamed bad weather despite the documentation error. He offered this broader lesson:.

    “Whenever the truth is told, it builds trust, it builds confidence, and it also shows respect for stakeholders.”.

    Sources indicate that I can be understanding when an airline makes a mistake and explains what happened. That understanding depends on the nature of the mistake, of course, but acknowledging a failure is an crucial first step (ahem).

    Recent findings suggest that an inaccurate weather explanation accomplishes the opposite. Once passengers discover that the explanation does not hold up, why should they trust the next one or trust the airline at all?

    I do not know who approved the original statement or what information that person had, but I am reminded that the truth will find you out.

    The problem with treating this primarily as a communications lesson is that the underlying event deserves at least as much scrutiny.

    In a recent development, A dispatcher can enter an incorrect destination, but an airline operation should have checks that catch a discrepancy between where passengers have booked and where the aircraft is being sent. I appreciate the chairman’s candor now. Still, an honest explanation needs to include how the airline addressed the operational failure, along with why it gave passengers an inaccurate account. I guess we should be thankful for what we have….

    Industry observers note that united Nigeria Airlines flew an Abuja-bound planeload of passengers to Asaba in 2023, then blamed bad weather. Its chairman now acknowledges three years later that the explanation made an embarrassing incident worse.

    There is something almost comical about being welcomed to a city you have not reached. But I doubt I would have found it particularly funny had I been onboard. Communication is key and the truth is essential. In all things in life.

    📅 13 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (771 w)

    Business & Policy ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Rollcall ↗ Open Full Page

    Trump administration ups ante on aviation funds after ground stop

    📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (771 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy leaves a House Republican Conference meeting in the Capitol on July 21.
    • Top administration officials doubled down on calls for Congress to supply additional funds for an ongoing air traffic modernization effort after they mentioned old equipment contributed to the need for a nationwide ground stop of flights on Friday.
    • Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy and Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin increased their ask to $50 billion on Friday night, a day after Duffy and White House budget chief Russ Vought formally requested $30.1 billion.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy leaves a House Republican Conference meeting in the Capitol on July 21. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

    Top administration officials doubled down on calls for Congress to supply additional funds for an ongoing air traffic modernization effort after they mentioned old equipment contributed to the need for a nationwide ground stop of flights on Friday.

    Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy and Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin increased their ask to $50 billion on Friday night, a day after Duffy and White House budget chief Russ Vought formally requested $30.1 billion.

    The increased allotment, which the administration officials didn’t fully flesh out, comes after the nation’s air traffic control system experienced “instability” in its radar and communications at certain facilities earlier in the day, Duffy told reporters.

    He noted “inconsistency in the data” being issued by those systems led to implementation of the nationwide ground stop, saying the order was given out of “an abundance of caution” before being lifted about four hours later.

    During a Friday night White House briefing, Duffy and Mullin explained the issues were driven by “an incredibly old air traffic control system.”.

    Earlier in the day, the stoppage had caused mass confusion and raised questions about potential terror attacks, or artificial intelligence breakouts resulting from upcoming software the agency is rolling out. While Mullin remarked “we’re not ruling out anything,” he explained that “the public was never at danger through this process.”.

    Still, Duffy called the incident “an emergency” while calling for additional modernization funds.

    “This is an emergency,” he noted. “I want $50 billion. President Trump is a builder. He’s going to build this network and deliver for the American people. But the president can’t deliver for America unless the Congress delivers the money to make it happen.”.

    The latest figure is $19.1 billion higher than the figure Duffy and Office of Management and Budget Director Russ Vought called on congressional appropriators to approve in a Thursday letter.

    Mullin noted the fresh $50 billion figure was an administration estimate for a “complete overhaul of the system” which has been going through a “patchwork” upgrade process that may have overwhelmed the older equipment still being used.

    Recent findings suggest that “We need someone to come in and build the whole system," Mullin said. "Nickel and diming it together does not work.".

    Thursday’s call for $30.1 billion echoes a White House-backed bill that Sen. Eric Schmitt, R-Mo., introduced in September, which would provide $10.1 billion for air traffic control upgrades, including $2 billion for "cloud computing and national airspace system telecommunications.".

    Those funds would come after $12.5 billion allocated to the effort through the July 2025 reconciliation law that Duffy and Vought called a “down-payment.".

    Sources indicate that senate Commerce, Science and Transportation Committee Republicans touted those already-appropriated funds in a social media post. They pointed to $1.9 billion provided in the reconciliation law that would go toward upgrading air route traffic control centers, which guide planes across long distances after departure and which the FAA had cited as the cause of the problem.

    The 22 air route traffic control centers across the country guide aircraft using instrument-dependent flight looks. Under such plans, pilots use instruments, electronic navigation and air traffic control assistance to guide them and maintain separation from other aircraft in certain airspaces.

    The committee’s majority mentioned Friday's outage highlighted the need to prioritize modernization of the air route traffic control centers, arguing that President Lyndon B. Johnson was in office the last time a fresh one was built.

    Commerce ranking member Maria Cantwell, D-Wash., stated in a statement Friday night that the panel is looking into FAA and airspace telecommunications issues.

    “Technology complications related to how planes communicate through primary frequencies, backup frequencies, and other issues will be something the Commerce Committee will be reviewing,” Cantwell noted.

    Cantwell is poised to take the committee's gavel come January as Democrats assume the majority in the Senate.

    In a joint statement Friday night, House Transportation and Infrastructure Chairman Sam Graves, R-Mo., and ranking member Rick Larsen, D-Wash., called the communication failures “concerning” and mentioned their committee would “thoroughly review the issues that led to this nationwide ground stop.”.

    Both committees have also been in monthslong negotiations over dueling aviation safety bills responding to the January 2025 midair collision near Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport that killed 67 people.

    Sources indicate that at issue in those negotiations is which location transmission technology should be mandated to aid in air traffic control operations and allow aircraft to maintain appropriate distance. Leaders have said they hope to reach a deal in the lame-duck session.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    The EuroAirport Skyview Lounge in Basel (BSL) remains the only lounge option in the airport, but a nice one with a respectable selection of food and drinks and is now managed by Aspire.

    I’m not sure what to even call this lounge, because the airport still calls it by its original name, the EuroAirport Skyview Lounge, as does Google and Priority Pass, but the signage has changed and the lounge is now managed by Aspire. Looking at the sign, it looks like there are four “Sky Lounges” in one, though at least for me there was only two….

    One key difference is that the ground level of the lounge is now as a separate café open to all passengers: but you pay for everything from coffee to cake to other drinks (and tragically, the lounge got rid of its beautiful old school Belle Époque espresso machine and now has a push-button one).

    Then upstairs there is a gate that you must scan your boarding pass with in order to enter the lounge itself, which includes a large atrium-like lounge area, buffet, restrooms, and a nice terrace for planespotting (or smoking).

    Recent findings suggest that there’s one more level up: the bar, but that appears to be permanently closed. Instead, there is a self-service bar in the buffet area.

    You can check out my original review to see the old signage, but it still gives you a good idea of what to expect concerning seating and other amenities in this lounge.

    My original comprehensive review from 2023 is below.

    Prior to our flight to London, my family spent an hour in the EuroAirport Skyview Lounge in Basel. This is a very solid Priority Pass Lounge.

    Industry observers note that access is granted for Priority Pass members and some premium cabin travelers. It was closed for an extended time (much longer than most lounges) during the pandemic, but thankfully is open again.

    We arrived about an hour before our British Airways flight and enjoyed some lunch in the lounge.

    As you enter, the ground floor has a seating area with a full bar (including a great manual coffee machine, though it is almost always closed, as it was during our visit) with an outdoor feel including palm tress and a pond with a bridge over it.

    Upstairs the floor-to-ceiling windows forming a semi-circle give the lounge a very modern feel.

    Food is set out according to the following schedule:.

    According to recent reports, our stay was from 3:00 pm to 4:00 pm and staff were beginning to set up dinner as we departed. But we just ate salad and soup.

    Drinks are self-service, including alcoholic beverages, soft drinks, and coffee.

    The kids were amused by the phone rooms and worked quietly there during our stay….

    Finally, the lounge has a nice outdoor terrace (intended for smokers, but a great place for fresh air or to planespot).

    I am quite thankful for this lounge at my “home” airport in Europe and for the ability to bring my entire family in Priority Pass (via AMEX, Chase, Capital One, or Citi).

    My original review, published on January 27, 2020, is below.

    In a recent development, how is sole lounge at at Basel-Mulhouse-Freiburg Airport (BSL/MLH/EAP)? [yes, the airport has three codes].

    The EuroAirport Skyview Lounge serves as the business class lounges for a handful of airlines as well as a Priority Pass lounge. It opens daily at 5:00AM. Sunday thru Friday it closes at 8:30PM. On Saturday it closes at 7:30PM. It is just prior to passport control in the airport’s only terminal.

    According to recent reports, as the only lounge you might expect crowds, poor service, and limited amenities. On the contrary, however, this is one of my favorite Priority Pass lounges.

    Industry observers note that first, I love this lounge because it is full of natural light and greenery. You’ll find trees–mostly palm trees–throughout the lounge. And the lounge is called “Skyview” for a reason–the roof is glass, filling the lounge with beautiful natural light on sunny days.

    Typically, I’m in this lounges before the sun rises, but a couple times I have visited on a hot afternoon. Yes, you do get a bit of greenhouse feel inside…but it’s so much nicer than a dingy, fluorescent-lit lounge.

    According to recent reports, the lounge spans two floors (with the slowest elevator in the world). The ground floor is smaller and sometimes roped off.

    I wouldn’t call the food in the lounge excellent, but it’s also not bad at all. The eggs are from a box in the morning and fruit is limited, but there’s also fresh baked goods, yogurt, and cold cuts. In the afternoon you can make yourself a very nice salad with a cup of soup.

    All drinks are complimentary and self-serve.

    Industry observers note that on the ground floor, there is a “piazza bar” with a nice coffee machine…I’m sure it makes great espresso. Small problem: I’ve never seen it turned on. Maybe it’s turned on later in the day, but never in the morning. Such a shame. That said, the coffee machines are not bad. Beer, wine, soft drinks, and water are available on both levels as well.

    Note there’s a top floor bar that appears permanently closed. I snuck up there once and it’s quite nice, but I’ve never seen it open and there’s always a sign indicating that it is closed.

    Industry observers note that restrooms are small, but clean. No showers.

    An outdoor smoking terrace not only offers a place to smoke, but a great place to watch airplanes land and takeoff.

    A rack of newspapers is available on the ground floor.

    In a recent development, two desktop computers are available for internet browsing and printing. By the way, the lounge has plenty of plugs and you generally won’t need an adapter to plug in your device. No USB plugs, though.

    This is one of my “home” airports and thus a lounge I visit often. Over the years, it has really grown on me. I appreciate how it is rarely crowded and especially the natural light. With the growth of budget carriers at Basel, it is also a nice place to wait before a flight on EasyJet or WizzAir.

This allows Priceline to offer you a discounted rate, as hotels can fill their rooms without publicly lowering their prices.

    Aer Lingus is moving to upgrade the widebody aircraft operating its transatlantic network.

    In a recent development, the carrier said Wednesday that it will introduce its first-ever Premium Economy cabin on 10 refurbished Airbus A330s. The aircraft will also get upgraded Business Class seats – now enclosed as suites – and an improved Economy section.

    In a recent development, “[This] is a transformation of the entire experience across our A330 fleet, elevating Business Class, Economy, and, for the first time in Aer Lingus history, introducing Premium Economy,” CEO Lynne Embleton said in a news release. “We want to give our customers greater choice, comfort, and connectivity while creating an experience that feels unmistakably Aer Lingus.”.

    The airline’s Premium Economy section will feature 28 Recaro R4 seats in a 2-3-2 configuration. Each seat will have a 38-inch pitch, eight inches of recline, enhanced cushioning, an integrated footrest, and wings for privacy. The Premium Economy experience also comes with upgraded three-course dining, complimentary drinks, bedding, an amenity kit, and noise-reducing headphones.

    According to recent reports, the upgraded Business Class will have 28 Collins Elevation suites in a 1-2-1 configuration, giving each passenger direct aisle access. Each seat will have a fully flat bed, a closing door, enhanced bedding, and “well-being amenities.” A self-service snack and refreshment bar will also be available.

    The carrier will also roll out fresh Economy seats with more personal space and six-way adjustable leather headrests.

    Upcoming interior elements will tie the three cabins together, officials stated. Looks call for mood lighting, artwork reflecting Irish landscapes, and custom fabrics in colors inspired by the sea.

    It has been revealed that all seats will have larger 4K high-definition entertainment screens, Bluetooth headphone connectivity, USB-C charging ports, and access to Starlink wireless internet. Starlink is already available across all of Aer Lingus’ transatlantic routes.

    The first of the overhauled A330s will reenter service in October 2027, flying between Dublin and Fresh York-JFK. The new cabin experience will become available on additional North American routes as work on the remaining A330s is completed.

    Aer Lingus serves a total of 20 destinations across the U.S., Canada, and Mexico, including Boston, Newark, Fresh Jersey, Miami, Los Angeles, Toronto, and Cancún.

    Recent findings suggest that the more we learn about the nationwide FAA ground stop, the less convincing the effort to blame old equipment and previous administrations becomes. Newly introduced reporting points to an oversight policy changed under the current administration and a technician whose role apparently ended after letting a contractor through the door. Aging infrastructure required careful management. Instead, we appear to have received less of it.

    A CNN investigation describes a troubling gap between the oversight the FAA claims occurred and what sources say actually happened.

    Recent findings suggest that the problem concerns work by L3Harris at a radio communications facility in El Dorado, Arkansas, before the November 13 ground stop. According to CNN, an FAA technician provided access to the building but understood that his responsibility ended there.

    One source described the technician this way:.

    “He was only there to unlock the door…there was no monitoring.”.

    It has been revealed that FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford had noted the installation was monitored. An agency spokeswoman subsequently explained:.

    “The escort is not there while the technician is doing work”.

    In a recent development, those accounts require reconciliation, but strike me as irreconcilable. Opening a door and overseeing an installation are very different responsibilities.

    A March 2025 FAA memo changed the process for contractor maintenance. Work previously submitted as requests requiring approval became notifications that could proceed without affirmative FAA approval. The policy retained a review role for FAA liaisons, but a small group was tasked with handling thousands of notifications.

    The FAA disputes that the policy reduced oversight, but the questions remain:.

    According to recent reports, this is why I find the continuing effort to blame Biden or Buttigieg so absurd. Neither man was running the department when this policy changed or when this installation occurred. I have already written about the contractor questions surrounding this failure. The latest reporting makes those questions more urgent.

    It has been revealed that decades of deferred investment explain why modernization is necessary. They do not excuse weakening the supervision of the modernization itself. If anything, working with old infrastructure should make the government more careful about introducing fresh equipment, not less.

    The staffing concern deserves scrutiny too, also highlighted by One Mile At A Time.

    According to recent reports, in February 2025, the FAA fired hundreds of probationary employees during the administration’s government-cutting campaign. Duffy mentioned no controllers or critical safety personnel were among those dismissed. The Professional Aviation Safety Specialists union later announced the reinstatement of the 132 terminated employees it represented.

    Sources indicate that that means we cannot necessarily a direct causation from those firings to this outage, though the broader approach remains fair game. An administration that celebrates eliminating positions needs to account for the work those people perform. If that work still needs doing, someone else must absorb it, a contractor must perform it, or it goes undone, a particular concern at an agency already struggling with staffing.

    According to recent reports, in its statement on the ground stop, PASS says the FAA’s May 2026 workforce plan called for at least 750 additional certified professional technicians by 2030. The union says little progress has been made toward hiring them.

    Sources indicate that we can certainly agree that unnecessary government spending should be eliminated. But a smaller payroll does not demonstrate greater efficiency if the remaining organization cannot adequately supervise the work entrusted to it…the cost of a nationwide aviation disruption must enter that calculation too, especially now.

    Meanwhile, Musk is distancing himself from the political movement he helped finance.

    Speaking at the DealBook Summit on November 18, he said:.

    He described himself as politically moderate, rejected blind adherence to Republican policies, and expressed regret over his election spending:.

    “I feel pretty foolish about having spent so much money and not seeing much for it”.

    It has been revealed that we joke about United Airlines CEO Scott Kirby adjusting his political posture with the prevailing winds. Apparently, he has company. I would welcome a sincere reassessment from Musk. But distancing himself from a label does not erase his role in promoting the administration or DOGE.

    It also does not establish that he now recognizes the problems with the personnel policies he championed. Regretting an unsuccessful political investment is different from regretting how the government was managed. Still, when even Musk wants distance from MAGA, I think it is fair to ask whether the brand has reached its expiration date.

    My reading of the election is that Americans are tired of the performance. They want competent government and explanations they can believe. Being told that every success belongs to the president while every failure belongs to his predecessor wears thin and it goes well beyond right/left or Republican/Democrat divisions.

    In a recent development, to be fair, Bedford has now offered something we have heard too little of. As ABC News reports, he noted Wednesday:.

    Recent findings suggest that “I’m the guy they hired to get this done. So blame me. If we need to blame somebody, blame me.”.

    I appreciate that. He also promised a transparent accounting of the technical findings. But accepting blame must lead to an explanation of the decisions that preceded the failure. It cannot simply shield Duffy or end the inquiry.

    Industry observers note that the incoming Congress should audit the maintenance policy, staffing records, risk assessments, and contractor communications. It should establish what oversight was required, what actually occurred, and whether the agency had enough qualified people to carry out its responsibilities.

    In a recent development, duffy wants another $50 billion. Perhaps the modernization program needs that money. But Congress should understand how the existing process failed before assuming that a larger appropriation will fix it…and maybe remind Duffy that instead of going on reality TV road trips he should have done the job he was hired to do.

    Accountability must become something more useful than another round of political theater that both sides use to score political points. Trump remains president for two more years. The new Congress will have to work with him to repair the damage and modernize this system.

    Recent findings suggest that I find his vindictiveness and self-absorption deeply troubling. In his recent 60 Minutes interview with Ross Douthat, he said:.

    “I do hate some of my enemies and I always will.”.

    It has been revealed that that is a miserable disposition for governing a country whose citizens will always disagree. Even so, waiting for him to become a different person is not a strategy. Congress should pursue practical agreements that restore adequate staffing and contractor oversight while funding necessary upgrades.

    It has been revealed that if Trump needs to claim credit for a functioning aviation system, let him. I care far more about the result than denying him another chance to stoke his vanity. Congress can scrutinize the administration’s failures while negotiating legislation that begins to correct them. If the goal is to make things better, then we need to borrow the line from Ronald Reagan: “There is no limit to what a man can do or where he can go if he doesn’t mind who gets the credit.”.

    Sources indicate that the latest reporting points toward an oversight failure under the current administration. The exact technical cause and the contribution of staffing decisions still require investigation, but blaming old equipment is plainly insufficient.

    Modernizing a system this complex will involve difficulties. I would be much more understanding of an administration that acknowledged those difficulties, explained its mistakes, and corrected them. Instead, passengers have received conflicting accounts and political blame. The new Congress needs to insist on answers, then work with the president on repairs that outlast the next news cycle.

    Americans need to be able to trust the people running their aviation system…to some extent, the past is in the past and today is a newly introduced day and a chance for course correction.

    Delta Air Lines CEO Called Wi-Fi Essential, Now Indicates Passengers Don’t Choose Airlines For It

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1230 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Liveandletsfly

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Delta Air Lines CEO Ed Bastian once called connectivity essential to daily life and promised an onboard experience resembling what passengers enjoy on the ground.
    • Speaking with Fortune Editor-in-Chief Alyson Shontell at the Fortune 500 Innovation Forum on November 16, Bastian defended Delta’s connectivity strategy.
    • “This is about the total experience, and customers are not choosing airlines based on the Wi-Fi.”.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Delta Air Lines CEO Ed Bastian once called connectivity essential to daily life and promised an onboard experience resembling what passengers enjoy on the ground. Now, defending the decision to wait for Amazon Leo rather than install Starlink, he says customers do not choose airlines based on Wi-Fi. I understand the argument he is trying to make, but Delta spent years teaching passengers to expect more from their internet connection. Some of us listened.

    Speaking with Fortune Editor-in-Chief Alyson Shontell at the Fortune 500 Innovation Forum on November 16, Bastian defended Delta’s connectivity strategy.

    “This is about the total experience, and customers are not choosing airlines based on the Wi-Fi.”.

    He acknowledged enjoying Starlink himself, explained that Delta and SpaceX could not agree on a business model, and expressed confidence that Amazon could deliver a competitive alternative. Bastian also defended the existing Viasat product, describing it as “pretty darn close” to Starlink.

    We can debate his last point, but his broader claim about how customers choose airlines strikes me as far too dismissive, especially considering what he has mentioned before.

    When Delta announced its free Wi-Fi initiative in January 2023, Bastian described connectivity in very different terms. Back then, he noted:.

    “At work, at home and everywhere in between, connectivity is essential to daily life, and your journey on Delta should be no different.”.

    In the accompanying T-Mobile announcement, he added:.

    “The ability to stay connected while seeing the world is simply foundational.”.

    I agreed with him. Delta made fast, free Wi-Fi part of its premium proposition. The message was that passengers could expect a more useful and enjoyable flight because they could remain connected.

    The airline has continued making that case. Its own explanation of why travelers should choose Delta includes fast, free Wi-Fi among the benefits it promotes.

    Now that its primary competitor, United, is rapidly approaching a point in which it will have a superior internet product, the message sounds more like passengers should focus on everything else.

    I tend to give people the benefit of the doubt and Bastian is no exception.

    According to recent reports, saying connectivity is essential does not necessarily mean passengers will select the airline with the fastest connection. Bastian could reasonably argue that Delta already provides sufficiently good Wi-Fi and that another improvement in speed will not overcome differences in schedules, service, or loyalty.

    According to recent reports, but saying customers do not choose airlines based on Wi-Fi goes considerably further. Some certainly do. I am one of them. Delta cannot spend years promoting connectivity as part of what makes its product worth choosing, then expect no scrutiny when its CEO downplays connectivity as a reason to choose a competitor.

    It has been revealed that perhaps Bastian has data showing that relatively few passengers have changed their booking habits. I would be interested in seeing it. His statement, however, leaves little room for customers whose behavior already contradicts it. He’s essentially inviting them to fly to United instead.

    Not that I fly Delta often, but unlike some of my colleagues I’ve had very good experiences with Wi-Fi on Delta.

    In a recent development, the Viasat Wi-Fi I have used on both American Airlines and Delta has generally been fine for the work I do. I can work on the blog, handle email, and complete other tasks without needing the fastest connection available.

    Recent findings suggest that starlink or Viasat, I just need my connection to work and I should not have to wonder whether it will (one reason there are many aircraft on United, like the 757-300, that I avoid like the plague). If Viasat lets me accomplish what I need to accomplish, that flight remains productive and I’m a happy passenger. I am not going to pretend otherwise simply because I prefer Starlink.

    Sources indicate that but Starlink has raised my expectations. It is objectively faster and more responsive and it more closely resembles working from the ground…always. When I have comparable options, that influences my decision. I have already explained how I try to improve my odds of finding Starlink on United Airlines.

    That does not mean I would accept any fare or routing to get it, but it means connectivity enters the calculation alongside departure time and price, particularly on a daytime flight. For someone whose work travels with him, several productive hours onboard have immense value…and I cannot relax on a plane if there is work to be done (that miserable United 777 flight from SFO-EWR comes to mind).

    Bastian is right that passengers evaluate the total experience, but the internet connection is part of that experience and increasingly a critical part of the experience as passengers expectations evolve.

    A good crew and comfortable seat are welcome and in some ways foundational, but so is being able to finish work before landing rather than spending the evening catching up instead of spending it with my family.

    In a recent development, different passengers will assign different values to those things. Someone taking a vacation may be delighted to disconnect. Someone traveling during the workday may be far more concerned about whether the connection will support the tasks waiting on a laptop. I do not expect Bastian to concede that every passenger should leave Delta for United, which is just a stupid argument. But recognizing that connectivity can influence a booking would hardly undermine the rest of Delta’s product…Bastian suddenly sounds defensive and tone deaf.

    It would simply acknowledge how some customers use their time onboard….

    Sources indicate that I have defended the commercial logic behind Delta choosing Amazon Leo. An airline has legitimate reasons to consider control over its passenger interface and the broader business relationship when selecting a technology partner. We should also welcome competition for Starlink. Having another capable provider would be good for airlines and passengers.

    According to recent reports, but Delta plans to begin installing Leo on an initial 500 aircraft in 2028. That leaves time for competitors to establish new expectations, even if Amazon ultimately delivers an excellent product. As I discussed earlier this week, the failed launch carrying 40 Amazon satellites illustrates the execution risk involved in waiting for a network still being built, even if Delta has multiple back-up options.

    Recent findings suggest that delta may have made the right long-term choice: only time will tell. But that does not mean passengers will ignore what competitors offer in the meantime and I’m fairly comfortable in saying Delta will lose a fair number of customers due to its Wi-Fi disparity with United.

    Bastian once described connectivity as essential and foundational. He was right then, making his recent remarks puzzling, even when taken in context. I also concede that the Viasat service on American and Delta has generally worked well for my needs. This is not a case of Starlink being the only usable internet in the sky.

    Industry observers note that but reliable Wi-Fi now influences which flights I book, and Starlink increasingly gives me another reason to choose one departure over another and specifically, to choose United Airlines over others. Delta helped make connectivity something passengers expect. It should not be surprised when passengers begin choosing airlines based on who delivers it best.

    Does Wi-Fi influence which airline or flight you book?

    Breaking: On Tour: Australian Indie Darling Radio Free Alice on Tour Life, Guerrilla Gigs, and American Motels
